metadata.title: Both Sets Scored 64
metadata.note: cli-explainer spine, weekly work report, claude-hai channel. Episode 3. Built to the PROOF rubric — FRAMEWORK (three questions about any emitted number: MEASURED OR SUBSTITUTED / DOES THE OUTPUT SAY / CAN YOU WALK IT BACK) shown before any example, steps 4 and 5 scored on it, and a falsifiability beat the framework PREDICTS and that calls back to episode 1 (the frozen corpus can reach only 5 of the 10 catalogue flags). Centrepiece is verified: clean and defective fixture sets both report overall_score 64. Every number from a live run — see SOURCES.md / FACTCHECK.md.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name. HAI short-form greeting.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane, and this is my week on Mycroft. Steps four and five are written. Together they produced the most uncomfortable number I have seen on this project.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the week's ask, answered

shot.show: the Claude composer with the week's ask and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "write steps 4 and 5: quality check, then a faithful port of the source workflow's sentiment scoring"
output: step 4 — flag, do not drop or coerce

beats.role_note: continuity with episode 2's ledger — kept tight so the FRAMEWORK lands near the first ~20s
beats.narration_text: Last week's ledger left three steps unwritten. This week two of them exist: quality check, and scoring. Scoring is a faithful port of the original workflow's arithmetic, and porting it honestly turned out to be the whole problem.
beats.new_visual_element: the series ledger, two more rows closing

shot.show: the six recipe steps, three already done, two closing now, one still open
shot.visual_intent: Six step rows. Steps 1-3 already ink with a tick. Steps 4 and 5 resolve from terracotta to ink and gain ticks. Step 6 stays terracotta and empty. The same ledger shape used in episodes 1 and 2, so the series reads as one project moving.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions about any emitted number, shown AS A STRUCTURE before either step is examined
beats.narration_text: Three questions to ask of any number a pipeline hands you. One: was it measured, or was it substituted — did data produce it, or did a fallback? Two: can you tell from the output which of those happened? Three: can you walk it back to the bytes it came from? Most dashboards answer none of the three. Everything after this is one of them.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: MEASURED OR SUBSTITUTED / DOES THE OUTPUT SAY / CAN YOU WALK IT BACK
shot.visual_intent: Three cards land in a row, one per narration step. They stay on screen as the rubric both steps are scored against, and the third is the one the trace chain answers.

beats.role_note: cycle 1 ask — SPARK-LINE LAW: greeting is the spark line
beats.narration_text: Step four. Deduplicate, and deal with the rows that are stale or wrongly typed. The obvious move is to clean them. Drop the stale ones, coerce the bad types, hand the next step something tidy.

shot.show: the Claude composer carrying the step-4 prompt

props.command: claude "write step 4: dedupe the shape-clean rows, and handle stale and wrongly-typed values"
output: two independent dedupe passes for news
wrong types flagged and LEFT as found

beats.role_note: THE ACTUAL-CODE LAW — step 4's own load-bearing rule, verbatim
beats.narration_text: It does neither, and the rule is written in the file. Flag, do not drop. Flag, do not coerce. A stale row is kept, because dropping it hides that the source returned out-of-window data. A wrong type is left exactly as found. And the reason is the step after it: the original turns parse-float of N A into a silent zero that reaches a sentiment score.
beats.new_visual_element: the FLAG, DO NOT DROP rule, verbatim

props.title: scripts/gigo/...-transform-quality-check.py
props.code:
FLAG, DO NOT DROP; FLAG, DO NOT COERCE:
    A stale row is flagged and kept, never silently dropped --
    dropping it would hide the fact that the source returned
    out-of-window data. A wrong-typed value is flagged and left
    exactly as found, never coerced.

    The source workflow's parseFloat(...) || 0 turns "N/A" into a
    silent 0 that reaches a sentiment score; the whole point of
    flagging here is that step 5 cannot make that substitution
    without it appearing in the record.

beats.role_note: cycle 1 output — the live step-4 run. MOVING, never a still.
beats.narration_text: Run it on the corrupted set. Five duplicate findings across four rows, and that gap is the point. News gets two independent passes: one on the id, one on the whitespace-normalised headline. One row trips both. Another has a different id, a different url, and the same headline — a syndicated copy that an id-only dedupe would count as two separate stories and double-weight. Then six flags: three stale, three wrongly typed. All of them kept.
beats.new_visual_element: the two dedupe passes, and what each one catches

shot.show: two dedupe passes side by side with the rows each catches, then the flag tally
shot.visual_intent: Two labelled columns held together: ID PASS catches three rows, HEADLINE PASS catches two; one row appears under both, drawn with a connector so the overlap is visible. Beneath, the flag tally: 3 stale + 3 wrong type, all marked KEPT in terracotta.

beats.role_note: THE REVISION LAW — cycle 2, the port
beats.narration_text: Step five is the port. Reproduce the original workflow's sentiment arithmetic exactly, so a reviewer can reconstruct any number the original ever produced.

shot.show: the Claude composer carrying the step-5 prompt

props.command: claude "port the Aggregate & Calculate Sentiment node faithfully — same arithmetic, including the JavaScript coercion semantics"
output: every substitution emits a named flag
no model call, no notification sent

beats.role_note: THE ACTUAL-CODE LAW — step 5's rule, verbatim. The reason NOT to fix the original is the teachable part.
beats.narration_text: Faithful port, loud substitutions. The original is not defensive. A missing price becomes zero. A stream with no rows scores fifty, which reads as neutral but is a default. The port does not fix either of those, because fixing them would change what the number means and embed a judgment no human has cleared. Instead every substitution emits a named flag, so a score built on one cannot be quoted without it.

props.title: scripts/tools/...-run-approved-tools.py
props.code:
FAITHFUL PORT, LOUD SUBSTITUTIONS:
    The original is not defensive: `parseFloat(x) || 0` turns a
    missing or non-numeric price into a silent 0, and a source
    with no records yields 50, which reads as "neutral" but is
    a default.

    Rather than fix these -- which would change what the number
    means and embed judgments no human has cleared -- every
    substitution emits a named flag, so a score built on one
    cannot be quoted without it.
props.sparkLine: Fixing it would change what it means

beats.role_note: cycle 2 output — THE CENTREPIECE. Both fixture sets report 64. Verified live.
beats.narration_text: And here is what that bought. Score the clean set: sixty-four. Score the corrupted set — five duplicates removed, six rows rejected, six quality flags raised — sixty-four. The same headline number. The arithmetic did not notice. What changed is the flag list: three flags on the clean run, eight on the corrupted one, including four rows that were flagged and still fed the score. The number is the same. The record around it is not.
beats.new_visual_element: two runs, one number, different flag lists

shot.show: clean and defective score panels both reading 64, with their flag counts beneath
shot.visual_intent: Two panels held side by side. Both show a large 64. Beneath each, the flag count: 3 on the clean run in ink, 8 on the corrupted run in terracotta, with 4 of those marked 'scored row carries a quality flag'. The identical number on both sides is the whole beat.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — the limit, predicted by the framework, and a direct callback to episode 1's frozen corpus
beats.narration_text: Now the limit, and it lands right back on episode one. The flag catalogue has ten entries. Run the entire frozen corpus through it and five of them fire. The other five never do — the coercions, the no-data default, the denominator mismatch. Those are exactly the substitution paths this step exists to catch, and the corpus that was built to make these validators gradeable cannot reach them. They were exercised in isolation instead. A test set that cannot trigger half your alarms is not evidence that they work.
beats.new_visual_element: ten catalogue flags, five reachable, five not

shot.show: the ten-flag catalogue split into reachable and unreachable by the frozen corpus
shot.visual_intent: Ten flag chips in a grid. Five resolve to ink and are marked FIRES. Five stay hollow in terracotta and are marked NEVER FIRES ON THIS CORPUS. Both halves held together so the ratio is visible while it is asserted.

beats.role_note: the ledger moves — what closed, what is still open
beats.narration_text: So the ledger. Five of six steps written. Eighteen of eighteen catalogued defects now detected at their exact locators, across steps three and four. The scores digest is stable across runs, and no-write creates nothing. Still open: step six, the report. And a scoring table whose weights and thresholds have no recorded author — flagged by the step itself, not by me.
beats.new_visual_element: the week's ledger — closed versus still open

shot.show: two-column ledger: closed this week versus still open, with the commit named
shot.visual_intent: Left column fills in ink: 5 of 6 steps, 18/18 defects at exact locators, scores_digest stable, --no-write writes nothing. Right column stays terracotta: step 6 unwritten, scoring weights unattributed. Kicker names commit 253ee74.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW + PROOF active-task rule — scaffold with a good/bad discriminator, read aloud
beats.narration_text: Your turn, and it is question two. Find a number your system reports to someone who trusts it. Paste this. List every value that was substituted, defaulted or coerced on the path to this number, and say whether the output shows that it happened. A good answer names a substitution and where it is disclosed. A bad answer tells you the calculation is correct — which was never the question.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the handoff prompt typed in

shot.show: the Claude composer with the viewer's prompt and the good/bad test

props.command: claude "trace this number back to its inputs. List every value substituted, defaulted or coerced on the way, and say whether the output discloses it."
output: GOOD: a substitution + where it is disclosed
a silent default is a number with no author
